title: Elusive ‘Geoneutrinos’ Are Building a New Map of Earth’s Volatile Interior
gist: Underground neutrino detectors (Kamland, Borexino, SNO+, and now China's 20-kiloton JUNO) are counting rare geoneutrinos to directly measure Earth's radioactive heat sources; site-to-site flux differences may hint the mantle is chemically non-uniform, possibly tied to LLSVP structures, but uncertainties remain huge. JUNO is expected to out-detect all prior experiments combined in its first year, and an ocean-bottom detector costing hundreds of millions may find funding in China.

insights.claim: After decades of searching, scientists have detected only a few hundred geoneutrinos in total: Kamland (Japan) first in 2005, Borexino (Italy) several dozen in 2009, and SNO+ (Canada) about 50 more reported in November 2025.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Illustrates how data-starved the field is and why new large detectors are a step change.
insights.quote: In November 2025, SNO+ reported its first detection, bumping up the number of observed geoneutrinos by about 50.

insights.claim: SNO+'s detections are the first geoneutrinos measured in the western hemisphere, giving a new geographic vantage on Earth's radioactive interior.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Geographic diversity of detectors is what enables mantle mapping.
insights.quote: These are the first geoneutrinos measured in the western hemisphere
insights.locator: What makes the detections at SNO+

insights.claim: SNO+ sits 2 km underground in Sudbury's Creighton mine and uses an acrylic sphere with nearly 10,000 light detectors and 780 tons of liquid scintillator, shielded by about 7,000 tons of ultrapure water.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Shows the extreme capital and contamination-control requirements of neutrino physics infrastructure.
insights.locator: This is the SNO+ neutrino experiment

insights.claim: China's JUNO detector, with over 20,000 tons of scintillator and operating since August 2025, is expected to detect more geoneutrinos in its first year than Kamland, Borexino and SNO+ combined over decades, and to report its first flux later this year.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: China is taking the lead in big-science neutrino infrastructure; expect data leadership to shift there.
insights.quote: expected to detect more geoneutrinos in its first year than the combined output of Kamland, Borexino, and SNO+ over decades

themes.theme: Earth's heat engine and mantle heterogeneity

insights.claim: Earth's interior heat comes from formation leftovers plus decay of uranium, thorium and potassium; without radioactive heating the planet would have cooled into a tectonically dead world.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Radiogenic heat underpins plate tectonics and the geomagnetic field, foundational geoscience context.
insights.quote: Without this second source, Earth would have long since cooled off and become a tectonically dead planet.

insights.claim: Best estimates suggest each detector site measures a different mantle flux, potentially the first hint that the mantle is not uniformly mixed, contrary to conventional geochemical assumptions.
insights.speaker: Mark Chen
insights.so_what: Could overturn a core geochemistry assumption about how radioactive elements are distributed.
insights.quote: It could be that that’s the first hint that the mantle is not uniform

insights.claim: The regions producing the most geoneutrinos sit roughly above the two continent-sized LLSVPs (under Africa and the Pacific), suggesting these deep structures may concentrate certain elements.
insights.speaker: Mark Chen
insights.so_what: Links particle physics data to seismology, potentially explaining origins of deep-Earth structures.
insights.quote: It could be that [they] concentrate some kinds of elements.
insights.locator: The regions that seem to be producing

insights.claim: Mantle geoneutrino flux appears very high at Borexino, very low at Kamland, and 'pretty in-between' beneath Canada at SNO+, though uncertainties are large.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Preliminary pattern that JUNO data could confirm or refute.
insights.locator: In general terms, the geoneutrino flux

insights.claim: Geoneutrino flux implies radioactive elements could supply anywhere from a small percentage to half of mantle heat, a discrepancy equal to the output of tens of thousands of nuclear power plants.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Shows how poorly constrained Earth's basic energy budget remains.
insights.quote: a discrepancy equivalent to the output of tens of thousands of nuclear power plants

insights.claim: Isolating mantle geoneutrinos requires subtracting high-energy particles, wrong-helicity particles, reactor neutrinos, and crustal geoneutrinos mostly from within a few hundred kilometers of the detector, making each estimate model-dependent.
insights.speaker: Ryan Bayes
insights.so_what: Results hinge on local geological models; discrepancies may be artifacts of counting methods.
insights.quote: They don’t just show up and say, ‘Hi, I’m a geoneutrino.’
insights.locator: The uncertainties associated with each detector

insights.claim: Researchers cannot yet tell whether flux differences reflect real mantle variation or differences in how experiments count geoneutrinos.
insights.speaker: William McDonough
insights.quote: Are the Italians right? Are the Japanese right? Are they both right? Or is something wrong?
insights.locator: If we take it at face value

insights.claim: SNO+ faces particular local-modeling difficulty from a 1.8-billion-year-old impact basin around the site.
insights.speaker: Virginia Strati
insights.so_what: Local geology complexity limits SNO+'s precision.
insights.quote: There are lots of unknowns in this geological area

insights.claim: An ocean-bottom neutrino detector, far from radioactive-rich continental crust and atop thinner uniform oceanic crust, would put measurements in 'mantle-only territory'; McDonough has championed it for decades.
insights.speaker: William McDonough
insights.so_what: Identifies the decisive future instrument for mantle chemistry.
insights.locator: Such a detector would be far

insights.claim: The ocean-bottom detector, estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars, has drawn little government funding so far, but McDonough hopes China, which has green-lit other big geoscience projects, will build it.
insights.speaker: William McDonough
insights.so_what: Signals China as the most willing funder of frontier big-science geoscience.
insights.locator: The idea of an ocean-bottom detector
